Unit 05 — Growth & Returns: why growth isn't always good

3 min read757 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06learn/unit-05-growth-and-returns.md

  2. ① Material — what we're learning
  3. ② Understanding — the idea in plain language

For a beginner. Starts Arc B (value & growth). New idea: growth only helps if it's profitable and durable — fast growth that loses money or rides a fad destroys value instead of building it.

Plain words first (read once)

  • Growth — sales (revenue) getting bigger over time.
  • Durable — lasting; not a one-time spike that fades.
  • Cash burn — spending more cash than you bring in (the opposite of generating cash).
  • Compound — stack gains on gains: profits reinvested that go on to earn still more profits.
  • Fiscal year — a company's official accounting year; some don't end in December (Peloton's ends June 30). · $X B = X billion. · A minus sign on a money figure (−$2.8B) means a loss.
  • Revenue / profit — money in from customers / what's left after all costs (Units 01–02).

① Material — what we're learning

Headlines love "revenue grew 120%!" But growth is a means, not the goal. The real questions: does the growth make a profit, and will it last? Growth that loses money just loses money faster; growth built on a temporary craze reverses when the craze ends.

② Understanding — the idea in plain language

Your lemonade stand does well, so you open a second stand. That's growth. Good or bad? - If each new stand makes money after its costs → growing is great; you compound. - If each new stand loses money → growing faster just loses money faster. Growth amplifies whatever the business already is. - And if sales spiked only because of a one-week heat wave, that growth isn't durable — when the weather breaks, sales fall back. A spike is not a trend.

The trap: revenue going up looks like success, so people fund "growth" that never earns a profit.

③ Example — Peloton (real figures; the COVID home-fitness boom and bust)

Peloton sells connected exercise bikes. When COVID shut gyms (2020–21), demand exploded — then reversed.

Fiscal year (ends June) Revenue Profit (net income) What was happening
2020 $1.83 B −$0.07 B COVID hits; home-fitness demand surges.
2021 $4.02 B −$0.19 B Revenue +120% in one year — the boom's peak. Still losing money.
2022 $3.58 B −$2.83 B Gyms reopen; growth reverses; a $2.8B loss.
2023–25 falling to $2.49 B still losing money every year The spike faded; never turned a profit.

Read it: - The growth was real but not good. Revenue more than doubled in 2021 (4.02 ÷ 1.83 ≈ 2.2× = +120%) — a number that thrilled headlines. But Peloton never made a profit, in the boom or after. - It wasn't durable. The surge rode a one-time event (locked-down customers). When gyms reopened, revenue fell and the losses ballooned to −$2.83B in 2022. - The lesson: explosive revenue growth that (a) never earns a profit and (b) depends on a temporary craze isn't value being created — it's a cash bonfire dressed up as success. Always ask of growth: is it profitable, and will it last?

④ Application — your turn

A. Compute (no computer needed). Revenue went from $1.83B to $4.02B. What's the growth %? (4.02 ÷ 1.83 ≈ 2.2, so about +120%.)

B. Judge it. A company's revenue triples in two years but it loses more money each year. Is that good growth? One sentence. (No — growth that loses money just loses money faster; it only helps if it's profitable and durable.)

C. Optional — pull it yourself (only if you have this project set up). python3 _ingest/edgar.py facts PTON — watch revenue rise then fall while profit stays negative. No setup? Skip; A–B taught the idea.

Check yourself

  1. Two companies grow revenue 30%. Company A earns a profit on it; Company B loses money on it. Which created value? (A. Growth amplifies the underlying business — profit or loss.)
  2. Why was Peloton's 2021 growth not a sign of a healthy business? (It never made a profit and rode a temporary, non-durable COVID spike that then reversed.)
  3. A company is profitable, but its sales jumped only because of a one-time fad that's now fading. Is that growth durable? (No — durable growth lasts; a fading fad-driven spike isn't, even if it was profitable. Growth must be both profitable and durable.)
